title: Ueda explains why Japan’s current-account surplus can persist without a trade surplus
summary: Japan’s current account has generally recorded a surplus of 2–4% of GDP for four decades. Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda argues that its persistence conceals a reversal in how Japan earns that income and who saves it. The goods surplus peaked above 4% of GDP in the mid-1980s and gave way to a deficit. Net primary income from abroad rose from negligible levels to more than 6% of GDP. A weaker goods balance therefore offers little guidance on its own about Japan’s external funding position or how much foreign currency Japanese investors will convert into yen. Ueda delivered the IMF’s Michel Camdessus lecture on 6 November. The Bank published it on 7 November (pp. 1–2, Charts 1–3).

The national accounts supply an identity: the current account equals national saving less domestic investment. They also pose a puzzle. Household net saving fell as the population aged, and the government ran deficits. Nonfinancial firms supplied the offset. After the late-1980s investment boom, asset prices and collateral fell while nominal debts remained due. Firms cut domestic capital spending, sold financial assets and directed retained profits towards debt repayment. In the late 1990s companies became net savers and maintained that position long after the acute banking crisis. In Chart 6, corporate saving rises relative to domestic investment. That gap helps identify who generated the surplus, although the chart alone cannot explain why these decisions persisted (pp. 2–5, Charts 5–9).

The destination of the money changed as firms recovered. Around 2011–12, domestic investment and borrowing started to rise again. Firms also bought and expanded businesses overseas. Direct investment’s share of outward financial flows increased from 21.0% in 1996–2011 to 46.5% in 2012–25. Portfolio investment’s share fell from 53.9% to 26.2%. Returns on foreign direct investment held above 8% for much of the period after balance sheets were repaired. When an overseas subsidiary retains earnings, Japan records the parent’s share as investment income and a matching outward direct investment. This accounting can support a surplus without any corresponding repatriation. The distinction matters for investors inferring yen demand from monthly external-balance data (p. 5, Charts 10–11).

Ueda questions whether a shortage of workers originally forced investment offshore. The Bank estimated an almost continuously negative output gap from 1993 to 2012, and unemployment averaged well above 3%. Participation by women and older workers increased employment over time. In his interpretation, executives anticipated fewer domestic customers long before they struggled to hire workers. A retrospective Bank survey found declining growth expectations prominent among explanations for weak investment. Managers also cited debt reduction, precautionary cash holdings and overseas acquisitions at different stages. These responses support the proposed sequence but cannot establish what firms would have done under a different policy response (pp. 5–8, Charts 12–13).

Actual labour scarcity now gives firms a reason to invest at home. More than 70% of respondents reported investing more actively in Japan in 2023–24 than previously, with labour shortages the most frequently cited reason. Automation, digital investment and relocating production could narrow the corporate saving surplus. Ueda also pointed to bank lending growth above 5%, the fastest in three decades apart from the 2020 period of government-supported lending. The stock of foreign assets and the return advantage on direct investment still support future income receipts. Whether stronger domestic spending will narrow the overall surplus depends on how much it exceeds corporate saving and how household and government balances evolve. Ueda gave no exchange-rate forecast or implication for the next policy meeting (pp. 6–8, Charts 9, 11–12).

questions.question: How much of the income surplus actually generates a need to buy yen?
questions.detail: The lecture shows why earnings retained by foreign affiliates appear on both sides of Japan’s external accounts. It gives no conversion ratio for dividends that are distributed. Use the Ministry of Finance’s balance-of-payments breakdown to separate reinvested earnings from dividends and interest, then examine company disclosures on repatriation and currency hedging. This would identify how much information the monthly primary-income balance carries for yen flows.

questions.question: Will labour-saving investment durably narrow the corporate saving surplus?
questions.detail: More firms report investing, but a survey response can cover anything from overdue replacement to a major capacity expansion. Compare realised domestic fixed investment and corporate saving in the national accounts with borrowing and outward direct investment. Separate industry and firm size where possible. A sustained rise in domestic investment relative to saving would be stronger evidence of external adjustment than faster bank lending alone.

questions.question: How sensitive is Japan’s income buffer to returns on the existing stock of overseas businesses?
questions.detail: Chart 11 divides investment income by the preceding year-end stock of each asset class. Persistent profitability, changes in geographical mix and exchange-rate valuation can affect the comparison. Examine Ministry of Finance income and international investment position data by category and region, alongside listed firms’ overseas earnings. This would help distinguish a fall in underlying profit from a currency translation effect when assessing the external balance.
